utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we begin in the usual manner by taking the appearances for today, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, Crispian Smith, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic for Zupljanin Defence. And I will take this opportunity to wish all the best to my learned friend Mr. Krgovic for his birthday today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Congratulations. I notice, Mr. Pantelic, that you embarrass Mr. Krgovic, but we join you. I understand that the -- Mr. Pantelic has a matter to raise but before he does that we have a brief oral decision and an announcement to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The oral decision is as follows. On the 19th of May, 2010 the Prosecution filed a motion seeking leave to add three items to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. On the 25th of May, the Trial Chamber granted the motion with regard to two of the items and remained seized of the motion with regard to Rule 65 ter 3598, a video containing one part of the an ABC Nightline news programme. The following day, the Chamber informed the Defence that it would be heard with regard to the remaining item. The time for such response has now elapsed without further submissions from the Defence. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the entire video broadcast is prima facie relevant, part of what is already in evidence. The Trial Chamber notes the Prosecution's assertion that it had intended to tender the complete programme but subsequently discovered that part of it, Rule 65 ter 3598 was missing from the version actually in evidence. The Prosecution will not seek to tender Rule 65 ter 3598, which has already been disclosed to the Defence before July of 2010. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the Defence will have sufficient time to deal with the video as they choose. Having considered all relevant factors for additions to the Rule 65 ter list, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that granting the request is in the interest of justice and, therefore, allows the Prosecution to add Rule 65 ter 3598 to its 65 ter exhibit list. And we have an announcement about non-sitting days. Further to discussions that have occurred in the course of this trial, usually at the instances of counsel for the Defence, the Trial Chamber has concluded that it will fix at least one but not more than two non-sitting days each month. Such occasional days will be settled by the Trial Chamber and the parties would be notified of the selected dates in such time as would facilitate their own planning. Accordingly, the dates so far determined are -- coincidentally, they're all Fridays, but that is not gospel for the future, but Friday, the 2nd of July; Friday, the 23rd of July; Friday, the 20th of August; and Friday, the 20th of -- Friday, the 10th of September. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of our clients with regard to their request requesting the health issues and actually request for this non-sitting days. Your Honours, I would like to bring to your attention the -- from my point of view, unacceptable practice of the OTP in process of disclosure and work so far. Yesterday during the examination of Mr. Njegus, examination-in-chief, my learned friend, Ms. Korner, spent a lot of time with him with regard to the issue of his contacts and some other aspect of the position of my client, Mr. Zupljanin. Contrary to the -- to the summary witness -- summary -- witness summary of Mr. Njegus, where in this summary, there is no word about Zupljanin. And in addition, we were -- we have been provided by Prosecution with a proofing note of Mr. Njegus prior to his testimony where only in one word our client, Mr. Zupljanin, was mentioned and that issue was clarified yesterday in accordance with the testimony of Mr. Njegus. Furthermore, on the 1st of June, information from interview of Mr. Njegus which was held on 24th and 25th February 2003 was disclosed to the Defence, which means after seven years. In addition to that, B/C/S version of that -- these notes were disclosed to the Defence on Friday, June 4th, 3.47 p.m. Now, the great surprise of the Defence is that why it takes seven years to file these particular documents. And while reviewing this information of the interview from 2003, on page 4, below the chapter or heading, under the title of cabinet meetings, we discovered that first two lines, which might be of importance, are deleted. So we don't know what is in this particular part, and we assume that it might be of interest to fulfil our Defence mission. I'm not speaking about the other parts obviously related to some footnotes or maybe remarks of the investigator, that's I'm not challenging at all, that's -- that's the work product of OTP team, but this particular sentence might have certain impact to ability to defend our client, and I kindly ask our friends to, as soon as possible, disclose us this particular part of this statement. Now, Your Honours, what we have here, we don't have, with regard to our client Mr. Zupljanin, nothing at all or -- or -- or very, very little in all these documents. But contrary to that fact, yesterday Ms. Korner was pressing, attacking, squeezing Mr. Njegus with regard to the issues related to my client. We all know how it was finished, as usual, without any grounds for their side. But the outcome of this problem, Your Honour, might be the following. Assuming during the Defence case that we shall provide to the Prosecution witness summary with the same standards and practice as they did, without any detail, without any -- any relevant portion to what we want to elicit or to lead our -- our witness. And then, suddenly, during examination-in-chief, we shall shift our strategy and we shall ask particular witness with enormous issues, which are not in the witness summary, and which are not in proofing notes. And then what? Where we shall be? I think this practice of Prosecution is a clear example of lack of due diligence, lack of professional diligence, and I kindly ask this Trial Chamber to issue a warning to the Prosecution with regard to this malpractice. Thank you for your attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I invite Ms. Korner to respond, the observation that I would make from what you would have said so far, Mr. Pantelic, is that, of course, the trial is conducted on the basis of oral testimony, if that isn't a redundant concept. In other words the -- what the Chamber hears at the end of the day is inclusive of documents that are exhibited. What the witness says and such summaries as would be provided in advance exactly that, a summary, because otherwise if it were merely a repetition in its entirety of what's -- of what's in the -- in the previous statements, the testimony would be redundant and we needn't come here and assemble, we could just read what the witnesses have -- would have prepared beforehand. Anyway, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honour, may I just be very brief. The point is that during proofing of Mr. Njegus, they were obliged to raise these particular issues that they will follow during the examination-in-chief otherwise this is clear attempt to -- to have -- ambush trial by them because what prevented them to ask him on May 13th -- 11 May, 13th May, and 6 of June to ask this witness certain issues regarding our client, which they did yesterday during the examination-in-chief. And then we might be entitled to -- to have the adjournment to discuss this new issues which we're not -- which was absolutely not -- not put in this proofing note and then to ask to consult with our client. That's -- that's my point, Your Honour. So we have to -- we are officer of justice. We have to fulfil obligations. We have to be fair, and -- and do our best in -- in our -- in our work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if I may presume to summarize what I understand Mr. Pantelic's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Pardon me? Yes, they're being caught by surprise. That seems to be the substance of his ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, I suppose it was rather foolish of me to imagine that Mr. Pantelic might actually read the interview on which basis we are calling this witness. Your Honour, the 65 ter summary is really an indication more to the Court than to Defence counsel of what is contained in already disclosed, for the large part, statements or interviews. The Court doesn't have perhaps the same facility and so that is why we put in the summaries. Your Honour, Mr. Njegus is being called on the basis of what he said in his interview in 2007. I will come to the -- the more legitimate complaint that Mr. Pantelic has about the late disclosure of the notes of interview in -- in 2003. Throughout that interview, and the part that I was attempting to get to yesterday, Mr. Zupljanin was mentioned by Mr. Njegus. Can I start with page 20 of the interview where he was asked to listen to an intercept, which I haven't troubled the Court with, the Court has had it before, between Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Stanisic, and he said: I recognise Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Stanisic's voice. He was asked a number of questions about the relationship on that page, at page 21, between Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Stanisic, which I was attempting to get to yesterday -- to get the witness to come to yesterday. Your Honours, we can put it up on the screen, if you like, if that helps. Properly quicker in Sanction than in -- oh. All right. 9035 -- sorry, it's 65 ter 9035. Then if you go over the page to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I -- I'm really sorry to interrupt. But I would need to object to this. I believe Your Honours gave the -- the floor to Ms. Korner to respond to what Mr. Pantelic have said. I don't think we need to go into the -- the actual evidence for -- for the purposes of -- of response, Your Honour, and showing the documents on that basis, I don't think it is appropriate. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the allegation, which is a serious one and which we take seriously, is that we have behaved improperly and that we gone beyond the scope of the 65 ter summary that we've led evidence that Mr. Pantelic was not informed of in advance, not by the interview, not by the proofing note. So I'm now entitled to show Your Honours exactly what that evidence is in the interviews, and I'm going, unless Your Honours stop me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- in the interests of time, the -- I suppose it may be useful to -- for us to be shown the particular examples, but the principle which Mr. Pantelic raises about generally being -- his word was ambush but the rule with which everybody is familiar about the entitlement of the Defence not to be taken by surprise. So if you could summarize your response to that. And as I said, the details we may need to come to because the remedy if -- if -- if a remedy is available to Mr. Pantelic, is that if, indeed, in the Chamber's view he was caught by surprise then he would be entitled to an adjournment to consider the new evidence, but that's -- that's the -- if you focus on that very narrow question --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope that is exactly what have I been doing, Your Honour, by taking you through everything single entry in this interview about Mr. Zupljanin. In particular, the part that I was attempting to address yesterday comes very early on in the interview. Page 22 - can we have that up, please - forget about the B/C/S. We just need the English. He is being asked why Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Stanisic were communicating during the blockade, and he says, he can conclude the following question by the investigator, I mentioned that Mico Stanisic was with the city SUP. He was sorry and he's correct himself, he was the advisor in the MUP but because of that position was he supposed to speak to Zupljanin. "A. Probably I know the following thing which happened after this. This happened after the 1st of April. When Mico was officially appointed minister, as far as I remember, Zupljanin at the very beginning even had a formal decision on his appointment as his deputy. He was at the same time the chief of CSB Banja Luka but as the deputy of Mico Stanisic too." And then he goes on to deal with how he knew Zupljanin on the next page. Your Honours, can I put it this way, there are ten or so different pages that deal with the witness's knowledge of Mr. Zupljanin, and he repeats again, later, in the interview, that he was under the firm impression that Zupljanin was formally deputy to the minister of the interior. The proofing note is meant to deal with matters that are not dealt with in the interview but are additional to other matters that the witness has mentioned. And in relation to that, and this is on the third page of the proofing note which I believe Your Honours have, he said this, because he said he discovered he made a mistake by talking to Mr. Macar and Mr. Planojevic. Whether or not there was an official appointment he felt that Stojan Zupljanin was Mico Stanisic's deputy. Stojan Zupljanin had a strong personality who was held in high regard in Banja Luka. As such he would have imposed his authority even more in a wartime situation. To say that they had no notice of the evidence which this witness was -- which -- I would have personally liked this witness to give, although he is clearly very reluctant to give it, is really a travesty of the actual situation, Your Honours. As I said to Your Honours before, there's a real difference between the Prosecution and the Defence 65 ters. We provide the 65 ter plus statements plus interviews plus massive disclosure. We get nothing from the Defence except for the 65 ter summaries and that's the difference between them. And as I say, the only way that Mr. Pantelic could have been taken by surprise is by not having read the interview or the proofing note. Your Honours, in respect of the note of interview that took place in 2003, Your Honours, it wasn't, as I say, as I led from the witness who feels very strongly about it and if required will explain to Mr. Pantelic about it, at that stage, in 2003, he was in fact the head of the administration, I believe, in the RS MUP, and he was seen by a lawyer and investigator on the basis, as he understood it, that it was an interview for information, that he wasn't being formally interviewed. There was no tape-recording, and regrettably, because of that situation maybe it didn't get into the system. When I was checking the interview for the purposes of calling Mr. Njegus, I saw there was a reference to an earlier conversation with the OTP. I therefore made inquiries. We did searches, and we discovered that there was indeed that record of interview. Not tape-recorded, not shown to the witness, not checked by him, and really as I understand the matter and certainly from the witness he understood that it was a conversation with him in his capacity as the then-head of the RS MUP, administrative section. So it can't be used by us as evidence but obviously it had to be disclosed. So at the last moment we got it translated. We disclosed it as soon as we found it. We then had it translated. In the e-mail which went with this document, we said, in terms, the only redactions that we have made to this are where they contain comments by the lawyer. They are not what the witness said. That is what the e-mail said. I noticed that Mr. Pantelic didn't mention that to you. What we redacted, because we didn't think what the lawyer thought was at all relevant, was the lawyer's comment under the -- the -- the heading cabinet meetings. I can assure Mr. Pantelic, and I'm perfectly prepared to tell him what the lawyer's comment was, if he really wants to know, but I don't see how it assists him, so that's the situation, Your Honours. It is unfortunate at that stage in 2003, Mr. Njegus doesn't seem to have been contemplated as any kind of a witness. I believe it was even before the arrest of Mr. Stanisic. He was being interviewed in fact by lawyers engaged on the Krajisnik case then I think for the purpose of information, but it didn't -- and therefore for some reason or another it didn't get into the system. So, Your Honour, that's the explanation. I hope that Your Honours will accept that explanation from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I was very precise in my submission. I said the footnotes I'm not challenging. That's the remarks. Let me -- let me just read this particular paragraph. Cabinet meetings, and then there is deleted part which is a part of information of that statement and certain -- certain -- certain facts by -- by Mr. Njegus, witness. Then after this deleted part in the middle of the page, we have the following; he states that they did not meet frequently because war activities has commenced and things were not centralised. He says that there was not much contact with the regions. So I assume with -- with significant ground that first part is -- contains certain names because the -- the -- the statements, sentence that I just read actually directs to that. I'm not speaking about footnotes where possible remarks of OTP team could be made. But this particular part I would like to have disclosed as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hear you Mr. Pantelic. Your Honours, I promise you, I was referring to that part. That was -- it starts with a lawyer's comment on what then follows, but I'm perfectly happy, as Mr. Pantelic clearly -- and I will show him the original document doesn't accept -- accept what -- what we say. It begins as follows in that paragraph: Njegus's comments in respect of cabinet meetings minimise the role of the cabinet and are most probably not reliable. I'm perfectly happy to show that to Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So for practical purposes the issue has been resolved. And we can get -- Mr. Zecevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of truthfulness, Your Honours, page 11, line 17, the -- the indictment against Mr. Stanisic was issued in 2005, and he was not arrested. He voluntarily surrendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was before Mr. Stanisic, in any event, had been indicted, and I should add, Your Honours, everything that is in that note effectively was repeated in the interview so that Mr. Njegus had a chance to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So counsel for both sides having had an opportunity to express their views on this issue, formally and on the record, we can have the witness escorted back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour. The allegation was, and I do think that in fairness to us you ought to say that you find no foundation, that we had not given the Defence advance notice of evidence that we were going to lead, and I think it is only right that Your Honours should say you don't find any foundation in that allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I appreciate your anxiety that the Chamber should so formally pronounce, Ms. Korner. But your articulation of your position and the historical overview of how you would have dealt with this matter seems to me to have put them -- to have -- to have dealt with the issue much more eloquently and accurately than anything that we could say, and I don't know that it would be of assistance for us to say anything more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I can say then, Your Honours, I would hope that in the spirit of co-operation and good relations between counsel, Mr. Pantelic might acknowledge that what he put forward, certainly in respect of the leading of evidence, was not totally accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... as he comes to appreciate the fullness of your explanation, that may be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Njegus, good afternoon to you. I remind you, before Ms. Korner continues, that you're still on your oath. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... Mr. Njegus, I want to go back --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to go back this afternoon to a question that His Honour Judge Harhoff was asking you yesterday. You were being asked questions about the -- the -- the document that showed that some kind of advisory staff was going to be set up. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Judge Harhoff asked you some questions about it because you said it was never actually brought into operation. And the question was by Judge Harhoff at the top of page 11301: "Your testimony is that it was just because of the fact that the head of the staff" -- who you said was Mr. Stanisic -- "never convened the persons who had been appointed, and that was the reason why it never became effective." Is that your testimony? And then for various reasons we moved on. Can I ask you now to answer that question, please. Is it because Mr. Stanisic never convened a meeting that this staff never became effective?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusion would be that that was the reason that that's why the staff never became effective. It is possible that there are other reasons, but I think that was the most important one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can't hear anything. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm having slight problems with my earphones today. All right. I'd like to move, please, then to ask you about another document in connection with this delegation of -- of authority to CSB chiefs and the like to appoint personnel. Could you have a look, please, at document -- it's 65 ter 2747.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 22 for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document of the 26th of April, 1992, and it's addressed to the five CSBs, the heads thereof. And if you look at the third paragraph, it says: "Bearing in mind the fact that the minister of the interior transferred his authorities to the heads of Security Services Centres in regard to the distribution of ... employees. I draw your attention to the fact the employment of the employees must be limited with the situation ..." And then: "All the decisions issued" -- in the next paragraph -- "so far by this ministry are still in effect and produce legal consequences. Proposals [sic] for personnel decisions." And then this: "However, in the future, heads of Security Services Centres will issue decisions for the employees within Security Services Centres and public security stations in their area and inform the ministry -- this ministry thereafter." And if we look, please, at the second page, which we already seem to, yeah, have. That's fine. Already in the B/C/S. Is that a genuine signature or facsimile of Mico Stanisic? Are you able to tell us? It's not very clear, I agree.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this. I am not familiar with the signature of Mr. Stanisic. It was not something one could see often. I cannot confirm whether this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honours, I'm so sorry, I can see why I can hear nothing because it's come apart. Sorry about this. That's it. It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you can't say whether it's his signature. What about the content of the document? Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, today after -- after -- after 18 years, I wasn't familiar with it before I -- had I had an opportunity to read this document, maybe I would have remembered the context. I'm sure it was drafted by several of us -- but I haven't had an opportunity to read it recently nor did I have an opportunity to read it two or three years ago, so I cannot be very precise about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... didn't you read it on Sunday? You went through all these documents I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand I should have read it, but I did not. There were many documents there, and I didn't go into the contents of it, and I just made decisions as to whether I'm familiar or not familiar with the document in the sense of the conversation we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, would you like to read through the whole document? I'm afraid -- I can hand you the copy. And if could just -- and see if you can tell us anything more about it. You say that -- you're sure it was drafted by several of you. Any of how, I'm sure the Court would give you the time to read through the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, perhaps before that, I'm a little bit confused about your question and the answer about the signature. You asked the witness whether he could say whether it is Mr. Stanisic's signature. If --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or a facsimile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or a facsimile.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Answer: I can't tell. But the witness recognised several times yesterday the facsimile, so he should be able to -- to recognise whether this is the facsimile or not, because facsimile is always identical, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honour probably is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, His Honour is absolutely right, and I would recognise the facsimile, but this is not the facsimile.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So is it Mr. Stanisic's real signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, his original signature was something one wouldn't see often. I didn't have many opportunities to see them often, and it's possible that it is, but it is also possible that it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would just like to have a quick read through the document then and tell us if can you say whether you drafted it or other people drafted it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too much time on this. This document is rather illegible, since it's a photocopy. But based on the content I cannot confirm with absolute certainty but it is highly likely that I took part in the drafting of it, possibly with someone else, because what's dealt with in this document is the issues related to personnel, an appointment of personnel. So I believe I may have taken part in the drafting of this document either directly or indirectly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was the purpose of this document, as we can see, to give more authority to the chiefs of the CSBs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. As I've told you yesterday, I'm certain that in some of the instructions that were sent to the CSBs, we kept talking about transfer of authority and that the authorities were, indeed, transferred upon them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe the witness should repeat his answer, because his complete answer has not been recorded. He was actually giving the reference to a time when this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Njegus, you heard that. Did you say at what period of time authority was being transferred? This document is dated the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the documents that was drafted during the month of April, and most probably not the only one such. There may have been other decisions where one can see that authorities were transferred from the minister to the chiefs of the CSBs, and -- and also to some other leadership structures within the MUP. I'm certain one of them was the chief of State Security Service and the commander of the special detachment of police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. The usher can give that back to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1420, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can I ask you now, please, to have a look at the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At a document, which is 363, please. 65 ter 363.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 29 - sorry - for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report dated the 8th of June, and it's a report on the status of personnel in the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic. And it's a quite a long report. It runs to - one, two, three, four - six pages in English. Yes, four pages in B/C/S. Did you read that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but only a glance. There's no need for us to dwell on that issue because I am familiar with the content of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then just two matters I want you to -- to deal with -- or three, first of all. Who actually drafted the report; do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I cannot remember with certainty, but I, either directly or indirectly, did take part in drafting of this report. Someone else may have also been included in addition to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This says -- the first paragraph, it says: According to incomplete and imprecise indicator, the records kept by the Serbian Republic, the ministry in June had 1.831 employees. And then somebody's written, obviously later, that it has been increased by the end of June to 2054, and that's without Banja Luka Services Centre. And then over the page in English, same page in B/C/S, third paragraph: "All employees are Serbian except six who are Muslim (five in Kalinovik, one in Ljubinje)." So between -- well, sorry, by the 8th of June, there were only, from your records, six employees of the MUP who were Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is slightly misleading. In this report it's not including CSB Banja Luka, so the question must be [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, look, I've already read that it excludes the CSB. It is obvious, is it not, that in the MUP, excluding the CSB Banja Luka, there were only six non -- six Muslim employees left in the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, two comments. This correction that can be found in the first paragraph, it is in my handwriting. I can confirm that the -- the data that was put in instead of the previous number is in my handwriting. Now I cannot tell you today whether this is or is not correct. However, since I most probably did take part in drafting of the report, I would say that my assumption is that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The addition that you did, was that to take into account Banja Luka? Because you didn't have it originally or -- on the 8th of June, but you added in, effectively, 200-odd further employees. Do you know how many employees Banja Luka CSB had?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from this vantage point, of course, I don't know that. I don't even remember why did I increase the number for the 200 or so. I can't remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I want to ask you anything more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1421, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next could you have a look, please, at document 1423.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tab 30A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document's going out under the name of Mico Stanisic, and it has a stamp. But do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is an order to the special police unit of the Ministry of Interior in Sokolac to carry out mobilisation. It's dated the 15th of June. Is that the same unit that we saw yesterday, that was headed by Malovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but I cannot confirm that today, whether this refers to his unit or to some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we saw -- it's -- it's -- this document is actually sent to the Sokolac Special Police Unit, and we saw yesterday the list of employees there. So are you saying there were two special police units at Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's not what I meant. My comment is about the order I have signed on -- for the minister after consultations. But one thing is certain, there were no two such units there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So you signed that order after you had consulted with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I think I didn't have any communications with him in relation to this order and this topic. It must have been with Cedo Kljajic that I have had consultations with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you said earlier was my comment about the order that I have signed on for the minister after consultations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. It hasn't been recorded. I wanted to get up but then I said, it wasn't recorded correctly what the witness said. Witness exactly said what he repeated in his next answer. Well, we can ask for verification, but I know what I heard. I wanted to -- to raise it, but I didn't want to interrupt Ms. Korner. Now it appears it's better that I should have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps we need to clarify this from the witness directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to, Your Honour. I -- I -- I really am a little unhappy about -- about what's going on in -- in questions of what's being interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You signed this order, it's your signature. There is only one special police unit which goes to Mr. Malovic with whom you would not have signed such an order, I take it, without authority from someone.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was explaining I think yesterday and also previously, what kind of situations one faced in relation to implementation of commitments and daily needs. This is yet another such example. I can confirm with full responsibility this is something I would have remembered since I have had very few conversations with Mr. Stanisic, the minister. In relation to signing of this order, I did not communicate with him. I signed it, I assume, in agreement with or having been ordered by security chief Cedo Kljajic. Whether the two of them had had any conversations about it, I cannot confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. How are you able to say about this particular, document, as opposed to many others that you may have signed, that you did not talk to Mr. Stanisic about it? What is it about this document that sticks in your mind that says, I did not speak to Stanisic; I spoke to Kljajic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to tell you things the way they were not. I was trying to explain yesterday and to the Prosecution in general that I have had very few contacts with Mr. Stanisic in person. Very seldom we had conversations. Very seldom I received orders from him. I would have remembered any order received from him because there were just a few of those. And that's why I can say that I did not have a conversation with him in relation to this particular order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an order for mobilisation. Could anybody except the minister of the interior have made -- given such an order?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, not who signed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I have to object, Ms. Korner. I don't -- I don't see how can you say that this is the order on mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we read --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I haven't read the English translation, but I know what it -- what it says in the Serbian original. That's why I'm intervening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The English original, if you look at that time on the screen, Mr. Zecevic, says: Order to the special police unit of the Ministry of the Interior (Sokolac unit) to carry out mobilisation of conscripts ... those who have not responded to the mobilisation in the Serbian municipality of, et cetera, et cetera. Now are you saying that is a mistranslation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying -- then what I'm saying is that you are misinterpreting the order. This is not the order for mobilisation. This is the order for arrest of the people who have not responded to mobilisation and bringing them to the military organs so they can mobilise them. That is the meaning of this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I'm glad you gave evidence, Mr. Zecevic, but perhaps we might just ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was this order that you were signing and let's -- let's concentrate on you're signing. You weren't signing in your own name and in your own authority, were you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were signing on behalf of Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... anywhere but it may be, of course the copy is so bad -- actually it is not that bad, the word "za." But it could be there, I suppose. All right. What does this order actually say? Forgetting about what Mr. Zecevic told you it said.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not forget that. The gentleman was correct in what he said. When I read what I signed, the purpose of this document was to convey to this special unit in Sokolac, to carry out the mobilisation of conscripts, who had failed to respond to previous call-up. That is the essence of what I just signed. Whether I had a right to or not is another matter. Just one more thing. You see this small letter Z, so the "za," for the minister, is there. That's also in my handwriting. The small letter Z in Roman script.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could anybody, other than Mico Stanisic as the minister, have given such an order?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's debatable now. Why not? Because it's obvious. We're talking about the month of June, right? Conscripts are not responding to mobilisation call-ups. The army is still not fully established. Police officers have to contribute, obviously, to the carrying out of mobilisation. And I'm sure that activities of this kind took place on the ground in most municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If you say that Cedo Kljajic was the one who gave you the instructions to send out this order and not Mico Stanisic, why, if anybody could make such an order, didn't it go out under his name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. It's possible that the man was just not there at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which man was just not there?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he wasn't there, and Mico Stanisic wasn't there, who gave the order to you to send out this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're coming back to the starting point again. My recollection is that I was instructed to this -- to do this by Cedo Kljajic, under-secretary for public security, who had the powers to issue such a decree, and since I signed it, I suppose that at that moment, the moment of signing, Cedo Kljajic was physically not present at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault, and it may be the question. What I meant was, if Cedo Kljajic had the authority to issue an order such as this, why did the order have to bear the signature -- the typed signature of Mico Stanisic and not that of Cedo Kljajic, whether or not Cedo Kljajic himself actually physically signed the document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the right question, and I can answer it. Most of the things that we issued from the locality of Vrace, most of similar documents, instructions, et cetera, went under the name of the minister, Mr. Stanisic. It's highly likely that not a single document went out under the name of the under-secretary, Mr. Cedo Kljajic. Most of these documents were signed minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that they were, and you're -- in fact, I can tell you, you're right, very little goes out under Mr. Kljajic's name, that we have. But what I want to know is, why does it bear the minister's signature and not of that Cedo Kljajic, unless it was the minister's authority that was required to give these orders? And I hope you understand that.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm just trying to explain what our practice was. The common practice was that everything issued from our offices in Vrace at the time went out under the name of the minister, not the others, the under-secretary for public security or the chief of administration. You will rarely find any documents signed by chiefs of administrations. Most of the documents were signed Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... try it another way. Was that because these documents, these orders, these dispatches, only had authority if they went out in the minister's name?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, certainly not. If anyone else had signed the documents, they would have had the same force.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I think we're getting -- I hope we can distinguish through the interpretation between writing, signing a document, and the typed signature. Whoever signed the document, physically signed with a pen, did it require, however, to have the name of the minister and his stamp in order for the document to have authority?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now if we look at this specific case, it's possible that somebody else's powers and signature would have sufficed. I'm just trying to explain to you the practice that prevailed at the time. The bulk of the documents that we drafted were drafted in this format, with the heading of the ministry, and under the name of the minister at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that was the practice. I'm not disputing that. I'm asking why. And you were a member of this ministry for a long time, Mr. Njegus. Why was that the practice?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it had been introduced at the beginning and then it remained in place. Now why it was introduced in the first place, it's hard to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Repeat for the final time and then I will move on. Was that because it required to have the typewritten name of the minister and the stamp for it to have any authority?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said no to this question. Similar documents could be signed by other senior officials at the base, at the headquarters, who would have enough powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think we tried, Your Honour, enough on this one. Your Honours, may that finally be admitted and marked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P1422, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Njegus, I'm not going to trouble you with the documents. But I think it's right that you attended on behalf of Mico Stanisic a number of sessions of the government, three in all. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right. Three sessions. And I was not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The purpose of sending you to those sessions was what?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what made the minister decide to send me to attend government sessions on his behalf in any one of the cases. In any case, I complied, I attended these sessions. I can only suppose that he sent placements because there was friction between him and the then-prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you report back on discussions at those meetings which affected the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I possibly did once. But in any case, nothing much was decided at government sessions regarding our field of work, with the exception of one session, which discussed the Law on Citizenship. Nothing else concerning the MUP was discussed at government sessions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to waste time because the Court has seen this but, in fact, wasn't there a discussion about the use of the Vila Bosanka in Belgrade; do you remember that, June ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't remember. And I don't know why it would have mattered to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, all right. Not to mention a discussion about who was entitled to wear camouflage and other uniforms in the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at document 1D0059. I just want you to identify the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that, and I recognise my signature, and I recognise the signature of Goran Macar who was either coordinator or acting chief of the crime investigation administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology. I misheard. The witness did not say apparently it was his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what you're asking me. There's no signature of mine here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. That's Mr. Macar's signature signing for Mr. Stanisic, is it, at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I confirm what I've just said, that Mr. Stanisic was mostly indicated in the signature place, and somebody else signed for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If you're about to go on to something else, perhaps we should take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I've just got two or three more documents to show you, Mr. Njegus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, first of all, document 221 -- yes, 218. 65 ter 218. Tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document, is that right, addressed to you for your personal attention -- yes. And it tells you there's going to be a meeting in Trebinje on the 20th of August. And this time, can you tell us, is that a facsimile, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think this is a facsimile. This is one of the few signed ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And so this meeting was considered important enough by Mr. Stanisic for him to have signed this document himself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if that was the reason why he signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But nothing could be more uninteresting, could it, given the number of documents that you say he didn't sign or didn't know anything about. Why would he bother to personally sign something telling you to attend a meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not the one who is supposed to make such conclusions. That's all could I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P01423. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And now can we look at the record, please, of the actual meeting, which is already exhibited as P163. If we turn, please, to the second page in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you're shown there, is that right, as an assistant minister, together with Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we clarified yesterday what my status was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, I'm just asking, why was it that everybody else had their appointments confirmed but you don't seem to have? This is August and you're still acting.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I did not get final appointment for what I was doing, in practice, but I continued to do that in practice and everybody accepted me in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look, please, now at some of the things that were said. At this meeting, Mr. Zupljanin was not present. Could you turn, please - one, two, three - to the fifth page in English and the fourth page in B/C/S. Mr. Cvijetic, I think it was, no, Mr. Savic, the Trebinje CSB chief was reporting and stated that in the Bileca area about 140 military-fit Muslims were arrested and were recently visited by the representatives of the International Red Cross. Did you understand for that that the reason for the arrest, from what Mr. Savic was saying, was simply that they were fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. But as I said yesterday, all of these broader major meetings took the following course. The chief of the public security station, each chief of the public security station, would give a briefing to those present about the situation in that area -- in his area. Of course, the chief of that centre found it necessary to inform the others of the problem he was facing in his area, Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, the question wasn't how the meetings went on. The question was: From what Mr. Savic said, did you understand him to be saying that they had arrested these Muslims simply because they were fit for military service, as opposed to having committed any crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What you did understand him to be saying then?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can't remember now. In any case, we misunderstood -- in fact, we did not understand at the time that they were arrested just because they were fit for military service. We understood that those were able-bodied military-age men and that there was a problem with a large number of them and the problem was what to do. I suppose after this meeting, some decisions were made as to how to deal with this problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you understand that these Muslims - I'm sorry to go on about this - had committed any crime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes; and, in part, there were men who could be a potential problem. Because many civilians at the time were already in possession of arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Was Mico Stanisic present throughout this -- this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, the meeting in Trebinje was divided into two parts. In the first part of the meeting, the minister was present. He did not attend the second part. The second part was chaired by Cedo Kljajic, then-under-secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll see later on that those you say rightly, there was a second part. So he was here when Mr. Savic said this?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would you describe Mr. Savic as a man with authority?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, as in the previous period, he was a man with authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did it ever cross your mind that he was the deputy minister to Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next can I ask you to look, please, at the -- in English, it is page 11, at the bottom, and in B/C/S, it is page 8. At least I think it is. Yes. The -- at the bottom paragraph in English and both in B/C/S and English says: "After the minister explained the reasoning behind the order to disband all special units in CSBs and SJBs, he explained the principles of further engagement of the special unit of the MUP police detachment?" What were the reasons that Mico Stanisic gave for the order to disband the special units?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't remember that. It was such a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then can we look at the minister of the interior's summary of the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go, please, to page 13 in English and, in B/C/S, to page 10. I'd like the third paragraph. Sorry, in B/C/S, oh, must be page 11. It says page 10 at the top n B/C/S. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "The internal affairs bodies have been infiltrated" -- he said -- "by individuals whose criminal and otherwise anti-social behaviour defiles the reputation of the MUP as a whole, and we must immediately rid ourselves of such individuals." Was that something that you personally were aware of, Mr. Njegus, that there were criminals and anti-social persons who displayed anti-social behaviour who were in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was exactly as is written here. This was a very good conclusion, like many others, I don't think this was debatable, and if the minister highlighted this as a topical problem, of which we were all aware, namely, that at the outset of the war there were people - not many of them - but, still, there were people admitted into the reserve force of the police who shouldn't have been. That is why, among other things, we held these meetings. And every time, if I remember well, fair and professional conclusions and decisions were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you were aware of this. And were you aware of this before August, in August, a long time before August?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we knew of it even before August. And we saw a minute ago the order written by -- signed by Mr. Macar that refers to the same thing. And we -- I'm sure we all remember that it was signed in -- in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: July, actually. But, never mind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've seen at this meeting and at the meeting in July, Mico Stanisic made some, as you put it, good -- I think the right words were "fair and professional conclusions and decisions." What exactly did he do himself to ensure that these decisions that were made were actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think, being a participant of the events at the time unfortunately, that everything was done that could be done at the time. Let's be realistic. As minister, he insisted on several things at every meeting of this type. To deal with the people who joined the police and should not have. He insisted on that at every meeting. And outside those meetings officially and unofficially. And what more can a minister do than issue orders and make decisions and demand that his subordinates do or act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you ever said to anyone that Mr. Stanisic, although he would make public pronouncement on policies by the MUP, he took few, if any, steps to ensure that his orders were carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. Could it be more precise, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you ever told anyone, not what you said here in court, but that, although Mico Stanisic would make public pronouncements on the policies, like these decisions we've looked at that were to be followed, he took few, if any, steps to ensure that those pronouncements, those orders, those decisions, were carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I ever said anything to that effect. Certainly not in such a context. I said what my impression was a short while ago and how I saw his attitude towards some matters of principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you point to any steps that he took after the meeting to ensure that those who had criminal records or who had committed crimes were thrown out of the MUP or prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what more than this do you -- do you want? What else should he have done?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did he go to visit the CSBs and asked for a copy of their records?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he went there; and, if he did, how often and where.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any reports, in your capacity as head of personnel, requested by Mico Stanisic as to the steps which had been taken in the SJBs or the CSBs to rid themselves of these criminal elements in the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There haven't been official written reports about that. Such reports were never made. But I'm sure that this item understood as an order was, indeed, implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what makes you so sure?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure because, as time passed, the MUP, as an institution, started working ever more professionally and -- and found a firm footing. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This meeting took place on the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the killings at Mount Vlasic, very, very shortly after the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's those famous Koricanske Stene. Of course, I heard. Everybody did but much later. At that moment, I knew nothing about it, and I believe that most of our members didn't have information about it either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that something you would have been -- would you have expected the investigation to have been pursued with all the resources available to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. One final thing on this meeting then, please. Could you look at item number 7, which is page 15 of the English, and page -- it's the twelfth page in B/C/S. This is still Mico Stanisic summing up. "The order to disband the so-called special units established by the CSBs and SJBs has been issued due to certain abuses." Now, that's a summary. Did he mention what those abuses were?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 18 years, I cannot remember all those details. I suppose - actually I'm sure - that this is a truthful summary, an accuracy summary, of all the conclusions made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the meeting at any stage told that there were allegations that members of these special police units had been involved in killing and looting and rape?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because I'm sure I would have remembered that. And it would have been a disaster if it had been the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were involved -- well, you gave the order for the disbanding of Malovic's special unit much later. At that stage, had you heard any allegations that they had been involved in crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because I would remember that, even after 18 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If they had been involved -- if you had heard any allegations they'd been involved in committing crimes, would you have simply agreed to disband them; or would you have tried to arrange for an investigation into these people?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just me. I don't know how much time we have, but I want to point out something to you. Most of us, or all of us, eight or nine of us, who were members of the collegium of the MUP were all serious people and good professionals. Most of us had never been -- or have never been in the SDS. I don't need to list all the names because they have been mentioned here, and you know them. I'm certain that I and most of them, too, would have spoken out publicly about that and would have done everything to launch an investigation into these events to shed light on them. Until the Prosecutor finds what she's looking for and asks her next question, let me add that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right. I don't want to stop you if you want to say something. I know what I'm going to ask next. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to add that for most of these crimes and silly events and that happened in those areas, we had no information about them. We learned about them much later. And in some cases we learned about them only after the war. That was, of course, our problem and the reason why adequate measures that should have been taken were not taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You're not telling us that you only learnt about the Vlasic mountain killings after the war, are you, Mr. Njegus?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even that is possible, or during the war at some point in time. I cannot now say exactly when. The people whose immediate area of responsibility that was know more about that. I know that an on-site investigation was conducted and some other police activities, but why that -- why the investigation wasn't carried out to the full, why it was broken off, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm asking you but when you learned about it. Didn't you learn about it almost immediately afterwards? Through, if nothing else, the outcry from the international press.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a solemn declaration yesterday, and I state with full responsible that, at that moment, I didn't know about that terrible event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you, then, about one last document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up, please, document P732, which is tab 7, I think. Yup.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now you were asked about this document which relates to the medals that people got during the course of the interview, and I just wanted you to describe the procedure as to how people were awarded these medals. Did -- who -- who proposed the people to be awarded medals?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this somewhat better. I remember the entire situation, and here's what I can say. In accordance with the then-Law on Commendations of the RS, that was the name of the law, if I'm not mistaken, the entire procedure was followed which, among others, includes all lower-level bodies of the MUP, submit their proposals with extensive reasonings, and that was done. I know that both police stations and the centres did that, as well as all administrations and the special police centres. So the full procedure was followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So all levels of the MUP could submit their proposals for those who got awards with, as you put it, extensive reasonings. Was that then submit to the MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there then a discussion about who should get a medal?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was Mico Stanisic involved in effectively making the final decision, in the consultations and making the final decision?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two versions of the event. But I would be more in favour of the version that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Hmm. And let's -- why do you say there are two versions; and why would you come down in favour of the one where he didn't get involved?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I took part -- in fact, I'm positive that he didn't -- wasn't involved in most of the procedure. He didn't sit with most of us from the MUP who drafted any proposals. He wasn't there physically or in any other way. And I don't believe that there was communication with him. I'm more in favour of that version, because Mr. Nenad Radovic on that evening when the proposal for the commendations was finalized left for Belgrade to verify it all with Mr. Stanisic, and after his return, he informed us that he did so. But according to the information I have, he never met him. That's why I'm more in favour of the version that Mr. Stanisic was not involved in making these proposals, and I don't believe that he took the final decision. But I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, how -- how would you like to fresh your memory about this from the interview that you had a couple of years ago with us? How about that, Mr. Njegus?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What's page 164 in ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Look at, please, in the B/C/S version, which you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's page 164 in English for counsel and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll put it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Korner. I have -- I have here the -- the interview of the witness, 23rd and 24th September, 2007 in Sarajevo. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Yup, at the bottom of page 164.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have the Serbian version. It only has 154 pages. It will take me sometime to find --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll give you the number in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 144, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You had the interview with you yesterday, Mr. Njegus. Have you got it today? Mr. Njegus, have you got your interview with you?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you didn't bring it today?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't brought it, but go ahead. You can interpret it; I'll remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can put it up on the screen for you. It's 146 in your language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have that up. What's the number of it? 9035, please. And in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have page 164 in English; 144 in the Serbian or B/C/S. 146, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's 147 that you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 147. All right. Page 164 in English and 146 in ... Can we move ... no. In English, 164. Yes. Thank you and apparently in B/C/S, 146. I don't ... okay. All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Do you see in the middle of the page, Mr. Njegus, the investigator asks you: "Now my question is you received the recommendation from the organisation. Then had you a meeting at MUP headquarters and they were finalized, narrowed down, and then sent out. Can you tell my whether Mr. Stanisic was also involved in these consultations and finalizing these recommendations? "Yes. "That these people should be awarded these medals? "Yes." Now, does that refresh your memory about what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry here. I'm sorry, Ms. Korner, but in all fairness to the witness you posed another question and then he gives the answer that he gave today on the next page, please. In all fairness to the witness, you should give him the whole context of his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I appreciate he -- later on says that Radic went to see Mico Stanisic, but I'm asking him about this answer here which is -- certainly to me, but -- I am certainly prepared to read the next bit about why he says Mr. Radic was the trusted man of Mico Stanisic, but can we deal with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you said "yes" there, what were you agreeing to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend, it's a correction. 44, line 23, it is not Radic. Who -- who is Radic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question now that you've had more time to think, Mr. Njegus. What was it when you said "yes" to those two questions that you were agreeing to?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here's what I can say. I believe that here too, as before, I have been sincere. I'm not saying that Mr. Stanisic was not familiar with the process and so on. That's what I meant when I said this three years ago. But then there was my statement that I made today and the statement that I gave three years ago. And what did I say? The same thing that I'm saying today, that I think that Mr. Stanisic was not the final authority to decide about these proposals. That's why I mentioned Radovic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. My original question was whether Mr. Stanisic was involved - and I'll go back to that - just a moment, Mr. Njegus. Don't speak until I've reminded you of what you said. I asked at line --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I suggest, Your Honours, that the Serbian copy of the witness statement, the -- the three relevant pages be handed over to the witness so he can refresh his memory. I think that's the only proper way to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Believe you me -- Your Honours, it is -- I would submit, completely unfair to be interrupted constantly during examination-in-chief in this way. When I have finished if it is thought that I have left something out, which I ought not to, then counsel can object. At the moment, I would be grateful if I may be allowed to conduct my examination-in-chief without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I asked you, sir, at line -- page 42, line 4, and I'll read from page 41, line 23: "So all levels of the MUP could submit their proposals for those who got awards with, as you put it, extensive reasonings and then submit them to MUP headquarters? "Yes. "And was there then a discussion about how should get a medal? "Yes. "Q. And was Mico Stanisic involved in effectively making the final decision in the consultations and making the final decision? "A. There are two versions of the event, but I would be more in favour of the version that he didn't, because I took part and, in fact" -- you then went on to say, I'm sorry, the question was: "Why do you say you there are two versions, and why did you come down in favour of the one where he didn't get involved because I took part, in fact, I'm positive that he didn't. He wasn't involved in most of the procedure. He didn't sit with" -- sorry. I lost it completely. In any event -- oh, for the days of binders. None of this ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "He didn't sit with most of us from the MUP who drafted any procedure proposals. He wasn't there physically or in any other way, and I don't believe there was communication with him." Right. Now, which is right, please, sir: That he took no part in these decisions at all, as you now say, didn't get involved; or, as you told the investigator in 2007, that he was involved in the consultations and finalizing those recommendations that people should be awarded these medals?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR NJEGUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My definite opinion is you can't have both, and as I've told you just a moment ago, I'm closer to believing my conclusion from before that he was aware of the process, the number of medals, hundred or 200 people. In that sense, I'm sure he was informed and aware of that. But whether he knew about details, names, that I don't know. How could I have known something like that? My conclusion, my personal conclusion, was that he didn't know about it, based on the unofficial information that I have about Mr. Radovic going to Belgrade and then telling us that the minister finally approved to complete the list. Much later I found out, and I still cannot claim with certainty whether that is true or not, so later I found out that he wasn't there with him at all. So, in the end, I'm more prone to believe that he did not see the minister, that he was not with the minister than the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
